c6_free_family.title: The long table
c6_free_family.text: Your cousin pushes the pie across the table and looks at her plate. “I should have said it differently, that day.” “Yes,” you say. Then you pass the bread, and that is how it is mended.

c6_free_quill.title: Quill counts
c6_free_quill.text: Quill counts every basket twice. “A tenth,” he says, and writes it with a small flourish. “The Lord will like the numbers. I like them better.” He looks at your fields as if they were a poem.

c6_free_greenstem.title: Two healers
c6_free_greenstem.text: Greenstem takes the chest in both arms. “Wren says I may carry it to the village myself.” Wren, behind him, folds her arms and does not say a word. Her eyes say a lot.

c6_free_miller.title: The wheel turns
c6_free_miller.text: The miller pours your flour into his hopper. He lifts the gate, and the stream takes hold of the old wheel. It creaks, then turns, slowly, as it did before the fire. “Hear that?” he says. “That is Hazelwood having bread again.”

c6_free_lark.title: Nutmeg
c6_free_lark.text: Lark holds out the cake. The squirrel takes it with both hands. “Nutmeg,” Lark announces. “Obviously.” The squirrel does not look as if it has any other opinion. You laugh until the fence shakes.

c6_free_garden.title: For the night garden
c6_free_garden.text: You set the bowl down at the edge of the garden. Far off, very softly, a very small bell rings twice. You nod, and walk home in the dark, and you are not afraid.

pages.text: In the morning you open the letter with the red seal. It is short. The Lord does not waste ink on farms. “Moonedge prospers. The share therefore returns to a half, as before.”
As before. You know that number. It is at the bottom of the burnt page, circled twice. Something old inside you sits up and stretches. Up before light. Bucket. Field. More. More. More.

A new trader has set up on the square, with a hat pulled low, a very red scarf and a coat with more pockets than anyone has counted. “Barter?” he says. “Yes!” He winks. You decide to stop wondering whose face is under the hat.

He wraps your cheese and whistles. He whistles your tune, every note, up and round and up again. At the place where it rests, he stops. He studies the cheese very closely. You wait. “Very good cheese,” he says at last, and pays far too much.

At dusk, on the first dry evening, the flowers open. White and small, with petals like paper, like the ones on your doorstep. Hundreds, one by one as the light goes, as if somebody were lighting a row of lamps. They were here the whole time. Under the water. Waiting.

In the very middle lies a ring of tiny silver thimbles pressed into the ground. Every one is full of water. Somewhere in the dark, very quietly, bells. Nobody comes out to meet you. You stand there a long time and do not say a word.

c6_fair_letter.title: We're coming to the Fair
c6_fair_letter.text: A last letter from the river barge: “We're coming to the Fair. All of us. Even your cousin.” You put it in your pocket and keep touching it all day.

c6_fair_tables.title: The tables fill
c6_fair_tables.text: The tables at the Fair fill up. Everybody brought something: Pieter a lantern cake, Greenstem a basket of mint, the miller, with a face like thunder, a sack of flour. The whole village works with you.

pages.text: That night the Wagon Players act the Ballad of Moonedge: a farm on a hill, a storm, lightning on the barn. Every child shouts “BOOM!” A child runs out of the burning barn crying “The lights! The lights!” The village sings along. You want to leave. You stay.

The Ballad ends. The village claps. Then, at the back, somebody stands up. It is Liv. “It wasn't lightning,” she says. She is looking at you. “You were in the barn that night. I saw you run out, crying about lights.” The whole square goes quiet.

You want to run. Instead you put the bucket down in the dust, in front of everybody, and sit on the nearest bench with empty hands. “Where were you?” asks Liv. “In the barn. Playing.” “Who with?” “I'm not going to say. Not here.”

“And the lantern?” “On the hook, outside. Then it was in the hay.” You swallow. “It went up as if it had been waiting. I hit it with the empty bucket. Then I ran, shouting about the lights. Nobody believed me. So I stopped saying it.”

Quill wants to write his real count, the one he keeps in pencil, in ink, in front of everyone. He cannot get the cork out. He tries his fingers, then his teeth, with dignity. Pieter takes the bottle, pulls the cork with his teeth, and hands it back.
Quill writes the third column on the Cloth Table, in ink, and signs it. “I have never written a number,” he says, “in front of the people it was about.” He hands the folded paper to Mayor Juno.

Juno reads it out. With Quill's numbers in hand, the Lord sets the share for Moonedge at a tenth, as in the old days. Nobody cheers, at first. Nobody quite believes it. Then Old Jan cheers, alone, very loudly, and then everybody does.

An alpaca stands at the gate, cream-coloured, very tall and very polite, with half a ribbon round her neck. The goat has eaten the rest. She looks at you for a long time. Then she lifts her head and hums one long, low note.

It is the note that woke the whole farm that night and got everybody down the hill. Nobody was hurt. Nobody at all. Because of her. She spits on the gatepost, politely, on principle. And the last line of the rhyme comes back, whole.

You say the whole rhyme out loud, from the very first line, to the alpaca and the goat on the roof and everybody: “Long ears sow the clover green, slow shell keeps the water clean, brave goat clears the bramble bed, strong pony brings the world its bread, wise badger heals what aches and stings, soft alpaca guards all things.” Your voice does not wobble once.

The supper is the long table in the square, under the lanterns, the whole village. You sit down at last. Nobody needs you to stand, or fetch, or carry. Then you get up once more, and lay one place at the end of the bench: plate, cup, spoon, bread.

On the low wall by the Hall steps sits Lark, swinging his legs. “There's a place,” you say. “Here.” He opens his mouth for the joke. It does not come. He sits down, carefully, as if the place might not hold him. “Nobody has ever set a place for me,” says Lark.

The goat eats the blue ribbon off the end of the table. “Is that a problem?” asks your mother. “No,” you say. Somebody starts to sing the rhyme, all six lines, to the old kitchen song. You know the tune. Your own hum slips in underneath, and fits.

c6_ajar.title: The edge of the night garden

pages.text: It is late. The Fair is over. You walk out alone to the white flowers. The alpaca follows, and stands with her back to them, facing the dark path, ready to spit at anything that comes up it. You turn your bucket upside down and sit.

“At the Fair I would not say who I was with,” you say, to the flowers. “It was you. You laughed at the bucket. You rode on the handle. One of your bells was cracked, and I never told you. You made lights. I laughed. And the lantern came in.”

“It got bigger, and I said it was all your fault. I said, go away. Then I told them it was you. That wasn't fair. I'm sorry.” Close by, in the flowers: Tink. Then, after a long time, two soft rings: Ting. Ting. You do not know what they mean.
The grandchildren are asleep, all but Minena. “Tell me the imp was real,” she whispers. You are quiet for a while. “Tonight,” you say, “I will start with the fire.”

And you say his name. Mumyo. Out loud, to a living person, for the first time in all those years. Then you tell Minena the truth, all of it: the barn, the lights, the bucket, the lantern on its hook. Quietly, the way it happened.

Halfway through you stop. “Are you tired?” asks Minena. “I am not,” you say, and fall asleep. Minena counts to ten on her fingers, very slowly. You wake up. “Where was I?” “The fire.” “Ah,” you say, and go on.

The room is very quiet. In the dented bucket on the windowsill lie Minena's stones, and a few flat grey ones that do not match. They are a little warm. “If you ever meet a little fellow with bells,” you say, “tell him I was never angry.” Minena nods, very seriously. That night she dreams of a melody, and in the morning she hums it.
